With scripting disabled, no automatic refresh occurs and the generation instant is shown.

SETUP-001.summary: Setup readiness: Setup asks the owner nothing Lamp can do itself.
SETUP-001.was: Setup readiness: Setup asks the owner nothing that Lamp can do itself (owner decision, 20 October 2026). Every change republishes the public page, and Lamp checks its own public page and subscribe form after each publish and on the minute Cron, reading the real rendered form, and checks a hosted sender with the mail provider when it changes and daily. Overview shows one line: the page is live at its address, when it was published and when the page and form were checked, with Review page (Your page, `/app/page`: Lamp's preview of the page, what it checked and ways to try it) and Change address (Settings). A failing check turns that line amber with a short reason and the one thing to do. Results belong to the address they were read from. The deployment address is the public address by default; a custom domain is optional. Local development suppresses outgoing mail, offers no captured-mail inbox, and prepares automatic one-click owner entry without email (owner decision, 15 October 2026). To prove a subscriber notice was produced locally, publish to an active subscriber, let dispatch run, and inspect its `suppressed` outcome in Notifications or `GET /api/app/deliveries`; `notification_deliveries` records that outcome without a provider-acceptance claim. Locally the sender is reported as email being off, never as verified; the hosted check reads provider authentication and does not claim inbox delivery. Public GET paths remain database-free.
SETUP-001.now: Setup readiness: **Requirement.** Setup asks the owner nothing Lamp can do itself. Overview reports the real public page and subscription checks, with an address-specific explanation and action when a check fails. **Acceptance.** 1. Every change republishes the public page; Lamp checks that rendered page and its real subscription form after publication and on each minute check. 2. Changing the hosted sender checks its provider authentication, and the check repeats daily. 3. Overview shows the public address, publication time and page/form check times; Review page opens the preview and its checks, and Change address opens Settings. 4. A failed check makes the line amber with a short reason and one action, and results remain attached to the address actually checked. 5. The deployment address is the public address unless the owner chooses an optional custom domain. 6. Local development suppresses outgoing mail, has no captured-mail inbox and gives the owner one-click entry without email. 7. Publishing to an active subscriber locally records a suppressed delivery visible in Notifications without representing it as provider acceptance. 8. The local sender reads as email off, and public reading remains database-free.

SETUP-002.summary: First-run setup: First-run setup begins with the owner's website and lets them edit what the site supplied before confirming the installed page.
SETUP-002.was: First-run setup: A signed-in owner whose installation has no stored first-run completion is sent from every operator document to `/setup`, which asks for their website first (owner decision, 20 October 2026). Lamp reads that public site once, refusing private and loopback addresses on every hop and running none of its scripts, and fills in what the site gives: page name, tagline, mark (stored as a PNG), accent colour and components from its navigation, plus the time zone from the browser; it never invents what the site did not give. When the site links to a Statuspage, Instatus or Better Stack page, or one answers at `status.<its domain>`, setup takes that page's own components and groups from its public feeds in place of the navigation's, labelled with where they came from, and offers "Bring its incident history too" (owner UI pass L11, 22 October 2026): off unless chosen, it imports the page's resolved incidents with their updates and times through Move in's keyless read, as MOVE-002's silent history; nothing open on that page, no maintenance and no subscriber comes, and a page whose feeds give no components changes nothing. A site that cannot be read, or no website, leaves plain defaults with one calm line. Every fact stays editable before and after; confirming stores the settings, the mark and the components and stores completion durably; afterwards `/setup` opens the app and settings remain editable in Settings. A signed-out visitor to `/setup` is sent to sign-in and returned there. An installation that already had an operator before this clause is recorded as complete by its migration. A setup rerun never clears completion.
SETUP-002.now: First-run setup: **Requirement.** First-run setup begins with the owner's website and lets them edit what the site supplied before confirming the installed page. The original setup decisions are recorded in RULINGS.md. **Acceptance.** 1. Every operator document sends a signed-in owner with no saved first-run completion to setup; a signed-out setup visitor signs in and returns there. 2. Lamp reads the public website once without running scripts, refusing private and loopback addresses at every redirect, and fills only observed page name, tagline, PNG mark, accent and navigation components, plus the browser time zone. 3. A linked Statuspage, Instatus or Better Stack page, or the site's status subdomain, supplies its own components and groups instead of navigation guesses, labeled with their source. 4. Bring its incident history too starts unselected; when selected it imports only resolved incidents and their updates at original times, silently through Move in, without active incidents, maintenance or subscribers. 5. A status feed with no components changes none; an unreadable site or omitted website leaves editable plain defaults with one calm explanation. 6. Confirming stores the edited settings, PNG mark and components and durably marks setup complete; all remain editable in Settings. 7. After completion setup opens the app; migration marks installations with a pre-existing operator complete, and rerunning setup never clears that completion.

SUB-001.summary: Subscribing: Visitors subscribe their own email address through the public page and receive confirmation before incident communication begins.
SUB-001.was: Subscribing: Submitting an email address on the public page creates a pending subscription and sends one confirmation email to that address within 60 seconds. That address receives at most one confirmation email in any 24 hours however many times it is submitted, which is what bounds a subscription-bombing attack. Unsubscribing through a link emailed to the address proves it is the subscriber's own and restores that allowance, so re-subscribing after unsubscribing sends a fresh confirmation. A pending subscription receives no other notification. The form is a standard POST that works with script disabled, is rejected with 403 when the request carries `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`, and carries no CSRF token, because with no cookie and no session there is no ambient authority to forge.
SUB-001.now: Subscribing: **Requirement.** Visitors subscribe their own email address through the public page and receive confirmation before incident communication begins. **Acceptance.** 1. Submitting an email address creates a pending subscription and sends one confirmation to that address within 60 seconds. 2. Repeated submissions give that address at most one confirmation in any 24 hours. 3. Unsubscribing with an emailed link restores the confirmation allowance, so a new subscription sends a fresh confirmation. 4. A pending subscription receives no notification other than its confirmation. 5. The form works with scripting disabled, refuses a cross-site submission and needs no ambient session or form token.

SUB-002.summary: Confirmation: Under the subscriber confirmation policy, only following the emailed confirmation link activates the subscription.
SUB-002.was: Confirmation: *Policy: `subscriber.confirmation.v1`; default: a subscription becomes active only when the link in the confirmation email is followed.*
SUB-002.now: Confirmation: **Requirement.** Under the subscriber confirmation policy, only following the emailed confirmation link activates the subscription. **Acceptance.** 1. A submitted subscription remains pending until its confirmation link is followed. 2. Following the confirmation link makes that subscription active.

SUB-003.summary: Pending expiry: Unverified pending addresses are retained only while confirmation remains possible.
SUB-003.was: Pending expiry: A pending subscription not confirmed within 72 hours is deleted, including the address it holds. **Supersedes BASE-DATA-002** for pending subscriptions only: the address was supplied by an unverified visitor who may not own it, so it is held only as long as confirmation is possible.
SUB-003.now: Pending expiry: **Requirement.** Unverified pending addresses are retained only while confirmation remains possible. Supersedes `BASE-DATA-002` for pending subscriptions because the submitting visitor may not own the address. **Acceptance.** 1. An unconfirmed pending subscription and its address are deleted after 72 hours.

SUB-004.summary: Component selection: Subscribers choose the components whose incident and maintenance communication they receive.
SUB-004.was: Component selection: A subscriber selects which components they want updates about, on the subscribe form or later on the management page, and the subscription follows exactly the components ticked (none ticked follows all), and is notified about an incident or maintenance only when it claims a state for at least one component in that selection. A subscription whose selection has never been narrowed follows every visible component, including components added after it was created. A subscription with a narrowed selection is unchanged when a component is added. When a component is attached to an unresolved incident, every subscriber who follows that component and has received no notification for that incident receives exactly one notification carrying its most recent published update, and then receives subsequent updates normally.
SUB-004.now: Component selection: **Requirement.** Subscribers choose the components whose incident and maintenance communication they receive. **Acceptance.** 1. The subscription form and management page preserve exactly the components ticked; no selection follows all visible components. 2. An incident or maintenance notifies a subscriber only when it claims a state for a selected component. 3. An unnarrowed subscription follows visible components added later, while a narrowed selection remains unchanged. 4. Attaching a component to an unresolved incident sends one latest-update catch-up to each eligible subscriber who has never received that incident; subsequent updates then arrive normally.

SUB-005.summary: Cookieless subscriber tokens: Emailed subscriber links carry opaque authority for one subscription, never a general login.
SUB-005.was: Cookieless subscriber tokens: A subscriber is identified on public surfaces only by an opaque token of at least 128 bits of entropy that addresses one subscription, is carried in the URL of a link the deployment emailed to that subscriber, grants no other capability, and is revoked when the subscription is deactivated or deleted. No cookie is set on any public surface. Responses on token-addressed paths carry `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` and `X-Robots-Tag: noindex`. **Supersedes BASE-PUBLIC-001** for token-addressed paths only, which transmit the token on load rather than after a first interaction, because SUB-006 requires an unsubscribe that completes without any interaction on our page.
SUB-005.now: Cookieless subscriber tokens: **Requirement.** Emailed subscriber links carry opaque authority for one subscription, never a general login. Token pages allow token transmission on arrival required by one-click unsubscribe; this supersedes `BASE-PUBLIC-001` only for those token-addressed paths. The technical profile is specified in [Delivery details](docs/contract/delivery-details.md). **Acceptance.** 1. A public subscriber token addresses one subscription, has at least 128 bits of entropy and grants no unrelated capability. 2. Deactivation or deletion revokes that subscription's tokens. 3. Token-page responses suppress referrers and indexing.

SUB-006.summary: One-click unsubscribe: Every notification offers standards-compatible one-click unsubscribe.
SUB-006.was: One-click unsubscribe: Every notification email carries a `List-Unsubscribe` header with a `mailto:` and an `https:` value, a `List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` header, and a visible unsubscribe link in the body. A POST to the `https:` value, with a body of `List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` in either multipart/form-data or application/x-www-form-urlencoded, deactivates that subscription and returns 200 with no redirect, no cookie, and no further interaction. Both headers are named in the message's DKIM `h=` tag, without which receivers decline to offer one-click at all. That endpoint's BASE-ACCESS-003 rate limit is counted per subscription token, never per source address, so one mailbox provider's shared egress cannot exhaust the limit for other subscribers.
SUB-006.now: One-click unsubscribe: **Requirement.** Every notification offers standards-compatible one-click unsubscribe. Its public rate allowance belongs to the subscriber token, so one mailbox provider cannot exhaust another subscriber's allowance. The technical profile is specified in [Delivery details](docs/contract/delivery-details.md). **Acceptance.** 1. Notification email contains the mail and web unsubscribe values, the one-click declaration and a visible unsubscribe link. 2. Both supported form encodings deactivate that subscription with a successful empty response, no redirect and no further interaction. 3. The message signature covers both unsubscribe headers. 4. One token's rate allowance never consumes another token's allowance, including requests from one mailbox provider.

SUB-007.summary: Managing a subscription: The emailed management link lets a subscriber manage its own channel and component selection without an operator session.
SUB-007.was: Managing a subscription: The token URL in every notification opens a page that shows the subscription's channel and component selection and lets the subscriber change the selection or unsubscribe, without a session.
SUB-007.now: Managing a subscription: **Requirement.** The emailed management link lets a subscriber manage its own channel and component selection without an operator session. **Acceptance.** 1. Opening the management link shows the subscription channel and saved component selection. 2. The subscriber can change its component selection and unsubscribe there without a session.

SUB-008.summary: Unsubscribe integrity: Opt-out takes effect for queued communication as well as future publications.
SUB-008.was: Unsubscribe integrity: After a subscription is deactivated, no notification is delivered to it. A notification committed before the deactivation and dispatched after it sends nothing and records the outcome as suppressed.
SUB-008.now: Unsubscribe integrity: **Requirement.** Opt-out takes effect for queued communication as well as future publications. **Acceptance.** 1. A deactivated subscription receives no later notification. 2. A notification committed before deactivation but dispatched afterwards sends nothing and records suppression.

SUB-009.summary: Webhook subscribers: A webhook destination and contact address receive complete, authenticated published events.
SUB-009.was: Webhook subscribers: An endpoint URL and a contact email address together subscribe as a webhook subscriber; the address exists so SUB-010 can say why the endpoint was deactivated. Each notification is a POST carrying `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, and `webhook-signature` headers, where the signature is a space-separated list of versioned HMAC-SHA256 values over `{webhook-id}.{webhook-timestamp}.{raw body}`, so a secret can be rotated without a gap. The body carries the incident, every update it has published, and each attached component's previous and new state, so a receiver that missed a delivery needs no prior state. It carries no subscriber address. A delivery succeeds only on a 2xx within 30 seconds; a redirect is a failure. An endpoint that is a Slack incoming-webhook URL (host `hooks.slack.com`) receives the same events, signed the same way, as Slack's message form: its text carries each bare `https://` URL from an update field as `<url>`, never `<url|text>`, and its rich-text link elements show the URL itself, so every field reassembles unchanged (UPDATE-013). Every other endpoint receives Lamp's format, whose update fields are the published text byte for byte.
SUB-009.now: Webhook subscribers: **Requirement.** A webhook destination and contact address receive complete, authenticated published events. The contact address exists for destination-deactivation notices. Slack incoming-webhook destinations receive Slack's message form; all others receive Lamp's form. The technical profile is specified in [Delivery details](docs/contract/delivery-details.md). **Acceptance.** 1. A destination and contact address create one webhook subscription. 2. Current and retiring signing secrets each verify the same complete event, allowing rotation without a gap. 3. The body includes the incident, every published update and every attached component's previous and new state, without a subscriber address. 4. Only a successful receiver response within 30 seconds counts as delivery; redirects fail. 5. Slack text keeps each bare secure-web URL bracketed with punctuation outside, never a labelled link; rich-text link labels are their URLs and each field reassembles unchanged. 6. Lamp-form update fields equal the published text byte for byte.

SUB-010.summary: Failing destinations: Destinations with permanent or repeated delivery failures deactivate with a recorded reason and receive no later notification.
SUB-010.was: Failing destinations: An address that hard-bounces once, or whose provider reports a spam complaint, is deactivated with that reason recorded. An address that soft-bounces on 5 consecutive notifications, and a webhook endpoint whose last 10 consecutive deliveries all failed under SUB-009, are deactivated with that reason recorded. Deactivating a webhook endpoint emails its contact address. A deactivated destination receives no further notification.
SUB-010.now: Failing destinations: **Requirement.** Destinations with permanent or repeated delivery failures deactivate with a recorded reason and receive no later notification. **Acceptance.** 1. One hard bounce deactivates the address and records the hard-bounce reason. 2. One spam complaint deactivates the address and records that reason. 3. Five consecutive soft-bounced notifications deactivate the address with that reason. 4. Ten consecutive failed webhook deliveries deactivate the endpoint with that reason and email its contact. 5. A deactivated destination receives no further notification.

SUB-011.summary: Operator view: Operators inspect all subscribers, their consent state and selected components, including deactivation facts.
SUB-011.was: Operator view: Operators see every subscriber with channel, state of pending, active, or deactivated, component selection, and the reason and time of any deactivation. Deleting a subscriber deletes the address or endpoint it holds.
SUB-011.now: Operator view: **Requirement.** Operators inspect all subscribers, their consent state and selected components, including deactivation facts. **Acceptance.** 1. Every subscriber is reachable, including records beyond the first page. 2. The view shows channel, pending/active/deactivated state, component selection, and deactivation reason and time. 3. Deleting a subscriber erases its email address or endpoint.

SUB-012.summary: No enumeration: The public subscription form does not disclose whether an address is already subscribed.
SUB-012.was: No enumeration: Submitting an address that already has a subscription returns the same status and body as submitting a new address and creates no second subscription. That address receives one email saying it is already subscribed, carrying its management link and nothing else.
SUB-012.now: No enumeration: **Requirement.** The public subscription form does not disclose whether an address is already subscribed. **Acceptance.** 1. Existing and new addresses receive identical status and body without creating another subscription. 2. An existing address gets one management-only email and no extra message content.

TEAM-001.summary: Equal operators: Operators share the owner role until TEAM-004 introduces its role matrix.
TEAM-001.was: Equal operators: Every operator can create, edit, publish, and resolve every incident and maintenance, change every component, and manage subscribers. There are no roles. The only gate on publishing is UPDATE-007.
TEAM-001.now: Equal operators: **Requirement.** Operators share the owner role until TEAM-004 introduces its role matrix. Review under UPDATE-007 applies on top of those common product privileges. **Acceptance.** 1. Every active operator can create, edit, publish and resolve incidents and maintenance. 2. Every active operator can change components and manage subscribers. 3. There are no differentiated product roles under this release’s operator model.

TEAM-002.summary: Management: Settings manages operator invitations and removal.
TEAM-002.was: Management: Operators are invited and removed in settings. The operator configured at setup can be removed only by themselves.
TEAM-002.now: Management: **Requirement.** Settings manages operator invitations and removal. The operator established during setup retains the self-removal protection. **Acceptance.** 1. A Settings invitation admits the invited operator into Lamp. 2. Settings can remove an operator. 3. Only the setup operator can remove their own protected setup identity.

TEAM-003.summary: Attribution: Lamp’s publication, state, maintenance, correction and subscriber-deletion records expose the acting operator privately.
TEAM-003.was: Attribution: Every published update, component state change, maintenance change, history correction, and subscriber deletion records the operator who made it. That operator's name is shown in the operator app and on no public surface.
TEAM-003.now: Attribution: **Requirement.** Lamp’s publication, state, maintenance, correction and subscriber-deletion records expose the acting operator privately. **Acceptance.** 1. A published update, component state change, maintenance change, history correction and subscriber deletion each records the operator who acted. 2. The acting operator’s name appears in the operator app and no public surface.

UPDATE-001.summary: Template: Updates describe customer impact and the next communication commitment in bounded plain-text fields.
UPDATE-001.was: Template: Publishing an update requires at least one attached component, an affected-audience statement of at most 250 characters, a customer-impact statement of at most 250 characters, and, for a lifecycle other than Resolved, a next-update time. A resolved update requires no next-update time and carries no next-update promise on any surface, including when an older stored resolved update retains a time. A what-still-works statement of at most 250 characters and a details statement of at most 500 characters are optional. Every field is plain text; no HTML or markdown is interpreted. A publish request that omits a required field, exceeds a length, or attaches no component returns 400 and changes nothing. The next-update time is a commitment to publish again by then; it is never presented as an estimate of when the incident will be resolved.
UPDATE-001.now: Template: **Requirement.** Updates describe customer impact and the next communication commitment in bounded plain-text fields. **Acceptance.** 1. Publishing requires an attached component, affected-audience and customer-impact statements of at most 250 characters each, and a next-update time unless Resolved. 2. Resolved updates need no next-update time and show no next-update promise on any surface, including older stored resolved updates retaining a time. 3. Optional what-still-works and details statements accept at most 250 and 500 characters respectively. 4. Fields are plain text with no HTML or Markdown interpretation apart from UPDATE-013’s bare HTTPS links. 5. Omitting required fields, exceeding lengths or attaching no component refuses publication without changing state. 6. The next-update time is a commitment to communicate, never a resolution-time estimate.

UPDATE-002.summary: One rendering: Wording stays consistent across public and delivery surfaces.
UPDATE-002.was: One rendering: The public page, the Atom feed, the widget payload, and the notification email render an update from the same renderer. No surface omits a populated field of the update or shows a field the update does not carry.
UPDATE-002.now: One rendering: **Requirement.** Wording stays consistent across public and delivery surfaces. **Acceptance.** 1. Page, Atom feed, widget and email retain every populated update field. 2. Each surface omits fields the update does not carry.

UPDATE-003.summary: Sets the lifecycle: Publication changes lifecycle and releases resolved claims together.
UPDATE-003.was: Sets the lifecycle: Every published update sets the incident's lifecycle state. An update that sets Resolved records the incident's end time and recomputes every attached component under COMP-006.
UPDATE-003.now: Sets the lifecycle: **Requirement.** Publication changes lifecycle and releases resolved claims together. **Acceptance.** 1. Every publication sets the selected lifecycle. 2. Resolved publication records the incident end time. 3. Resolved publication recomputes every attached component under COMP-006.

UPDATE-004.summary: Preview: Before publication the composer previews the customer-facing update.
UPDATE-004.was: Preview: Before publishing, the composer shows the update as the public page and as the notification email will render it, produced by the renderer named in UPDATE-002.
UPDATE-004.now: Preview: **Requirement.** Before publication the composer previews the customer-facing update. **Acceptance.** 1. The composer shows the update as the public page renders it. 2. The composer shows the update as the notification email renders it.

UPDATE-005.summary: Drafts: Private drafts survive reload without reviving obsolete publication wording.
UPDATE-005.was: Drafts: An unpublished update appears on no public surface. A draft is saved within 2 seconds of the last edit and is restored unchanged after a browser reload. Publication consumes that draft and opens an empty draft for the next update, with lifecycle prompts. A stale tab cannot resurrect published wording or overwrite a newer acknowledged draft. Draft writes, template application, scheduling and publication require the acknowledged draft version. A fresh empty composer is not reported saved until a native write is acknowledged; Publish requires a complete acknowledged draft. Reconciliation after a lost acknowledgment identifies the attempted write and preserves later workflow changes.
UPDATE-005.now: Drafts: **Requirement.** Private drafts survive reload without reviving obsolete publication wording. **Acceptance.** 1. An unpublished update appears on no public surface. 2. The last edit saves within two seconds and reload restores it unchanged. 3. Publication consumes the draft and starts an empty next-update draft with lifecycle prompts. 4. A stale tab cannot resurrect published wording or overwrite a newer acknowledged draft. 5. Draft writes, template application, scheduling and publication require the acknowledged draft version. 6. A fresh empty composer claims no save before native acknowledgement, and Publish needs a complete acknowledged draft. 7. Lost-acknowledgement reconciliation identifies the attempted write and preserves later workflow changes.

UPDATE-006.summary: Scheduled publish: A scheduled update stays private until its committed publication time.
UPDATE-006.was: Scheduled publish: An update given a future publish time publishes within 240 seconds of that time and appears on no public surface and in no notification before it. If UPDATE-007 review is in force and the update has not been reviewed when that time arrives, it is not published, stays a draft, and is reported under NOTIFY-006. The 240-second bound is a declared promise based on one local stress observation with 20 updates and 20 maintenance starts due in the same cron minute on a single workerd process on a shared runner; it is not a p95 over independent runs or a hosted Cron guarantee.
UPDATE-006.now: Scheduled publish: **Requirement.** A scheduled update stays private until its committed publication time. **Acceptance.** 1. A future-dated update publishes within 240 seconds after its time. 2. Before its time no public surface or notification carries it. 3. Under the owner’s review policy, an unreviewed due update stays a draft and raises a NOTIFY-006 operator notice.

UPDATE-007.summary: Review: The owner chooses whether a second operator reviews updates.
UPDATE-007.was: Review: *Policy: `update.review.v1`; default: no review is required. When review is required, a publish request for an update its author wrote is rejected with 409 until an operator other than the author marks it reviewed; the reviewer and the time are recorded on the update.*
UPDATE-007.now: Review: **Requirement.** The owner chooses whether a second operator reviews updates. **Acceptance.** 1. Under required review, an author’s unreviewed update is refused until a different operator reviews it. 2. The update records reviewer and review time. 3. When review is not required the review policy does not hold publication.

UPDATE-008.summary: Atomic publication and recipients: Publication commits its fixed recipient set before dispatching without holding publish.
UPDATE-008.was: Publish is atomic: One transaction commits the update together with the recipient set it will notify on each channel selected under NOTIFY-007. That set is fixed at publish time: a subscriber who narrows their selection afterwards still receives this update, and one who unsubscribes afterwards does not, per SUB-008. When the publish request returns 200 that transaction is committed, and PAGE-007 and NOTIFY-002 follow from it. When it returns an error the update is on no surface and no recipient is recorded for it. Dispatch of the committed set is retried until it succeeds and never blocks the publish.
UPDATE-008.now: Atomic publication and recipients: **Requirement.** Publication commits its fixed recipient set before dispatching without holding publish. Its committed success starts PAGE-007’s visibility bound and NOTIFY-002’s delivery bound. **Acceptance.** 1. The selected channels’ recipients and the update commit together before success is returned. 2. Narrowing selection afterwards preserves committed delivery; unsubscribing suppresses it under SUB-008. 3. Failed publication exposes no update and records no recipients. 4. Dispatch retries the committed set until success without blocking publication.

UPDATE-009.summary: Templates: Operators save and apply reusable wording and component choices.
UPDATE-009.was: Templates: An operator can save a template holding the update fields of UPDATE-001, the components it attaches with the state each claims, and the lifecycle state it sets. Applying a template fills the composer and attaches those components with those states, and publishes nothing.
UPDATE-009.now: Templates: **Requirement.** Operators save and apply reusable wording and component choices. **Acceptance.** 1. A template retains UPDATE-001 fields, attached components with their claimed states, and lifecycle. 2. Applying it fills the composer and stages those choices without publishing.

UPTIME-001.summary: Definition: The public uptime figure derives from component-state history over the trailing ninety days.
UPTIME-001.was: Definition: For each visible component the page shows the percentage of the reporting window during which the component was not in a downtime state, computed from COMP-003 state history at one-minute resolution and rounded down to two decimal places, so a window containing any downtime never shows 100.00%. The reporting window is 90 days.
UPTIME-001.now: Definition: **Requirement.** The public uptime figure derives from component-state history over the trailing ninety days. **Acceptance.** 1. Each visible component shows the percentage of the ninety-day window not in a downtime state, using one-minute resolution. 2. The figure rounds down to two decimals so any downtime prevents a displayed 100.00%.

UPTIME-002.summary: Downtime weights: The owner-replaceable downtime policy weights affected minutes consistently with the displayed incident history.
UPTIME-002.was: Downtime weights: *Policy: `uptime.downtime-states.v1`; default: a minute in Major outage or Partially unavailable counts as one downtime minute, a minute in Degraded performance counts as half a downtime minute, and a minute in Under maintenance counts as none.* Degraded performance is not weighted at zero: most published incidents never get worse than it, and discarding them is what makes an uptime figure disagree with the incident history printed beneath it.
UPTIME-002.now: Downtime weights: **Requirement.** The owner-replaceable downtime policy weights affected minutes consistently with the displayed incident history. **Acceptance.** 1. The supplied weights count Major outage and Partially unavailable as one downtime minute per minute, Degraded performance as one half, and Under maintenance as zero.

UPTIME-003.summary: Short history: Uptime begins only where state evidence exists and labels short coverage honestly.
UPTIME-003.was: Short history: A component whose earliest state history entry is later than the start of the reporting window shows uptime computed from that entry, and the page labels the figure with the coverage: elapsed hours and minutes while it covers less than one whole day ("less than 1 minute" below a minute), and whole days from one day onward. A component with no data says No data (owner S4, DIVERGENCE.md "Public page clarity").
UPTIME-003.now: Short history: **Requirement.** Uptime begins only where state evidence exists and labels short coverage honestly. Under RL-2, short coverage does not invent a whole day. **Acceptance.** 1. If recorded history begins after the reporting-window start, uptime is computed from that first record. 2. Coverage under one day is labeled in elapsed hours and minutes, with less than 1 minute below a minute; from one day it uses whole days. 3. A component with no data says No data.

UPTIME-004.summary: Corrections: An operator corrects a closed history interval with an attributable reason while retaining original facts.
UPTIME-004.was: Corrections: An operator can correct a closed interval of a component's state history, stating the correct state for that interval and a reason. The correction appends to the history per COMP-003, recomputes every uptime figure it affects within 60 seconds, and records the operator, the interval, and the reason in the audit log. A request without a reason is rejected with 400.
UPTIME-004.now: Corrections: **Requirement.** An operator corrects a closed history interval with an attributable reason while retaining original facts. **Acceptance.** 1. The operator supplies corrected state, closed interval and reason; omitting the reason is refused. 2. Correction appends a superseding history fact rather than changing the original. 3. Every affected uptime figure is recomputed within sixty seconds. 4. The audit records operator, interval and reason.

UPTIME-005.summary: Stated method: The initial public page explains uptime weights and window beside its figures; every published incident contributes through its component claims.
UPTIME-005.was: Stated method: Beside the uptime figures the page names each state's weight under UPTIME-002 and the length of the window under UPTIME-001, in text present in the initial HTML. Because UPDATE-001 refuses to publish an update that claims no component, every published incident moves these figures; none of the incident history printed on the same page is invisible to them.
UPTIME-005.now: Stated method: **Requirement.** The initial public page explains uptime weights and window beside its figures; every published incident contributes through its component claims. **Acceptance.** 1. Initial HTML names the selected weight of each state and the reporting-window length. 2. No published incident is invisible to uptime: publishing requires at least one claimed component.

UPTIME-006.summary: Daily record: The page displays each visible component’s daily record without inventing coverage before history begins.
UPTIME-006.was: Daily record: The page shows one mark per day of the reporting window for each visible component. A day containing any downtime minute is labeled with the number of downtime minutes in that day. A day before the component's earliest state history entry is rendered as having no data and is visually distinct from a day with no downtime.
UPTIME-006.now: Daily record: **Requirement.** The page displays each visible component’s daily record without inventing coverage before history begins. **Acceptance.** 1. One daily mark covers each day of the reporting window for every visible component. 2. Any downtime day labels its weighted downtime minutes. 3. Days before tracking begins are labeled No data and visually distinct from a zero-downtime day.

TEAM-004.summary: Roles: Lamp defines Owner/Admin, Communicator, Responder and Viewer privileges and protects its last Owner.
TEAM-004.now: Roles: **Requirement.** Lamp defines Owner/Admin, Communicator, Responder and Viewer product privileges and keeps its last Owner recoverable. This replaces TEAM-001’s common owner role; review under UPDATE-007 remains additional. **Acceptance.** 1. Owners and Admins manage settings, team, integrations, pages and billing-relevant providers; Communicators publish, resolve, schedule maintenance and manage subscribers. 2. Responders draft, write internal notes and attach components without publish rights; Viewers only read, including private pages. 3. A Responder’s publish is refused while a Communicator publishes that same draft, and a Viewer cannot change Settings. 4. The setup operator is an Owner and the last Owner cannot be demoted or removed. 5. Every role refusal has an audit record naming operator, requested action and time; role changes appear in the audit view with actor and time. 6. Only Owners and Admins can read the audit log; a Communicator is refused.
